title: Vishvamitra and the prayer for a stirred mind
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a king loses to a sage's staff, and the Gayatri asks for one thing
carry: the gayatri asks one thing: stir our minds
tomorrow: the Gayatri's first word points. at what, exactly?
last: LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.

lines: TEN PAST SIX. THE KETTLE ISN'T ON.
TWO. ONE IS OURS. ONE IS HIS.
cards: Ten past six, a kitchen in New Jersey, the kettle not on yet. Nani stands at the window with her eyes half shut, saying the same three short lines she says every morning.

Priya leans in the doorway in a hoodie, holding a printout. The school's winter assembly wants each senior to share one line from their own tradition, and Priya has written GAYATRI at the top and nothing under it.
She waits for Nani to finish. Then: Nani, where's the verb? Nani smiles.
There are two, she says. One is ours. One is his.

teach.h: A KING LOSES TO A SAGE'S STAFF.
teach.b: Nani's answer starts with a story, because this verse has a seer, and tradition names him Vishvamitra. Before he was a sage, he was a king.

In the Ramayana, King Vishvamitra rides with his army into the forest home of the sage Vasishtha, and the sage feeds every soldier from one wish-granting cow. The king wants her. He offers a hundred thousand cows.
Vasishtha says no. So the king takes her by force, and loses: the cow calls up warriors of her own, and when Vishvamitra throws every weapon he has, Vasishtha's plain wooden staff swallows them all.

The king stands there with nothing and says, more or less: shame on a warrior's strength; a sage's power is the real power. He walks away from his throne to find it. Now the verse he's remembered for.
Tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. Find the verbs.
Prachodayat: may he stir. In plain English: we hold in mind that radiance of the god Savitr, worth choosing; may he stir our thoughts. And here's the teaching.

teach.h: NOT RAIN, NOT WEALTH, NOT VICTORY.
teach.b: The Gayatri doesn't ask for rain, or wealth, or victory.

teach.h: IT ASKS FOR A MIND MOVED.
teach.b: It asks that the mind be moved by a light beyond it. That's why so many Hindus say it at dawn and dusk, and why many families give it to a child first, at the sacred-thread ceremony.
Of everything a person could ask for, the tradition puts this one first.

how: Many Hindus say the Gayatri at dawn and dusk, and in many families it is taught at the sacred-thread ceremony; traditions differ on who chants it, some keeping it for those who have received the thread and others teaching it to all. Tradition names Vishvamitra as its seer.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a king who won a sacred cow by force and kept her
a king who became a sage, and a verse that asks for a stirred mind
a sun hymn that asks for rain and good harvests

p: the king who became the Gayatri's seer
the sage whose staff swallowed every weapon
the people's verb: we hold in mind
the god's verb: may he stir

tradition names Vishvamitra, a king who became a sage, as the Gayatri's seer
the Ramayana tells how he gave up his throne after losing to Vasishtha.
Vishvamitra won Vasishtha's cow by force

games.q: Priya gets one sentence at the assembly to say what the Gayatri is. which sentence is true to the verse?
o: a prayer for success in the year ahead.
a prayer that the god's light stir our minds.
a hymn asking the sun for good weather.
games.why: two verbs: we hold the radiance in mind; may he stir our thoughts. it asks for a mind moved, the thing a king gave up his throne to find.

practice: On any scrap of paper, write the two verbs far apart: dhimahi on the left, prachodayat on the right. Under the first write we hold in mind, under the second may our thoughts be stirred, and draw one line joining them.
Then rest your eyes on the page while the time runs.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants, read word by word. Today, the map: two verbs, and a king who learned what's worth asking for.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Gayatri, the name the verse is known by.

carryVoice: Your line: the Gayatri asks one thing: stir our minds. A king gave up a throne to learn that, and of everything Nani could ask for at ten past six, it's the one she asks first. See you tomorrow.
